stops.name: Ecbatana, the dream of Astyages
stops.campa: In the seven-walled city of the Medes, Astyages the king dreams of his daughter Mandane. Water pours from her until it floods all Asia; the Magi read a warning and marry her low, to a quiet Persian, Cambyses of Anshan. Then a second dream: a vine grows out of her womb and overshadows the whole of Asia. The Magi speak plainly now: her son will reign in the king's place. Astyages sends for Mandane, heavy with child, to keep the birth under his own eye. The vine is already reaching for his throne.
stops.quote: A vine grew from the private parts of his daughter, and overshadowed the whole of Asia.

stops.name: Ecbatana, Harpagus is given the child
stops.campa: The child is born. Astyages calls Harpagus, his kinsman and most trusted man, and commands him to carry the infant home and kill it. Harpagus takes the boy, weeping, and will not do it with his own hand: the child is of the royal blood, and the king is old and sonless; the crown may yet pass to Mandane. He summons instead the king's herdsman, Mitradates, and lays the deed on him: expose the infant on the wildest mountain, where the beasts will finish the king's order.
stops.quote: Take the boy whom Mandane has borne and carry him to your house and kill him.

stops.name: The Zagros pastures, Mitradates and Spako rear the child
stops.campa: The herdsman climbs to his hut in the high pasture, dreading the order. His wife Cyno, Spako in the Median tongue, the She-Dog, has borne a dead child that very day. She kneels to him: do not cast a living royal boy to the dogs and birds; let our own dead son lie exposed in his rich swaddling, and we will raise this one as ours. So it is done. The stillborn is shown to Harpagus's men as the king's grandson; the living heir grows up a herdsman's son on the mountain, and the tale will later say a she-dog suckled him.

stops.name: The village of the herdsmen, the boy-king game
stops.campa: At ten, playing in the road, the village boys choose him king. He rules in earnest: some he sets to build, some to be his spearmen, one he names the King's Eye. When the son of Artembares, a Median noble, defies an order, the boy has him seized and whipped. The bruised child runs to his father; Artembares storms to Astyages demanding justice: a herdsman's brat has flogged the son of a great house. The king summons the boy, looks on the frank, unbending face, and something moves in him: the features are his own, the age fits the deed done ten years ago.
stops.quote: Master, I did it, and justly; for the boys of the village, of whom he was one, made me their king in their play.

stops.name: Ecbatana: Astyages knows his blood, and the feast of Harpagus
stops.campa: Under threat, Mitradates confesses all. Astyages, told by the Magi that the prophecy is spent, since the boy already reigned, in play, sends Cyrus home to his true parents in Persia. But on Harpagus he takes a horror of a revenge: he butchers Harpagus's own son, serves the flesh at a banquet, and after the eating shows the father the head and hands in a basket. Harpagus bows, gathers the remains, and says only that whatever the king does is well. In his heart he begins to wait.
stops.quote: Whatever the king does is pleasing.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 1.119 (Harpagus, having eaten his son)

stops.name: Anshan, the son of Cambyses comes home
stops.campa: The boy comes down out of Media to the old Elamite citadel of Anshan, to Cambyses and Mandane, and learns whose son he is. Here is the house of Achaemenes and Teispes, kings of Anshan under Median overlordship, keepers of the fire and the mountain. He grows to manhood among the Persian tribes: the Pasargadae, the Maraphii, the Maspii, herders and horsemen of the uplands, hard men of a hard country. The vine that Astyages dreamed is rooting itself in Persian soil.

stops.name: Anshan, the message hidden in the hare
stops.campa: Cambyses dies; Cyrus is king of Anshan, still a vassal of his grandfather in Ecbatana. From Media, Harpagus sends a courier: a huntsman bearing a hare, its belly sewn shut over a letter. Cyrus slits the beast and reads: the Medish nobles hate Astyages and will turn if Cyrus rises; strike, and I will bring the army over to you. Harpagus has waited nine years for this. Cyrus lays his plans for revolt against the greatest power of the age.
stops.quote: If you will listen to me, you shall rule the land over which Astyages now reigns.

stops.name: The Persian tribes assembled, the day of thorns and the feast
stops.campa: Cyrus gathers the Persians and sets them a day's labor clearing a thorn-choked waste, brutal, back-breaking toil. Next day he feasts them on slaughtered flocks, with wine and every good thing, and asks which day they preferred. All choose the feast. Then, he says, choose me: obey me and you have days like this and freedom besides; refuse and you have endless labors like yesterday, under the Mede. They swear to follow. He raises the standard of revolt.
stops.quote: If you will be ruled by me, you will have these good things and ten thousand more, with no servile labor; but if you will not, you will have labors like yesterday's without number.

stops.name: The plain of Hyrba, first blood against the Medes
stops.campa: Astyages, hearing of the rising, arms the Medes and, in a madness the historians call god-sent, puts Harpagus in command of the very army meant to crush Cyrus. The hosts meet. According to the tale of the frontier, the Persians hold against the first Median assault; the war will run three years. Harpagus and a great part of the nobility, as promised, go over to Cyrus in the field. The Median host breaks apart from within.

stops.name: Ecbatana taken, Astyages in chains
stops.campa: In the third year Cyrus routs the last Median levies near the field that will become Pasargadae, and takes Ecbatana itself. Astyages is led out a prisoner to the grandson he ordered killed as an infant. Cyrus does not kill him; he keeps the old king by him to the end of his days. The seven walls with their coloured battlements, the treasure of the Medes, the empire, all pass to the Persian. The vassal is now the master; Media and Persia are one crown. The Babylonian Chronicle records the day: Astyages taken, Ecbatana plundered, the spoil carried to Anshan.
stops.quote: He mustered his army and marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan... The army rebelled against Astyages and he was taken prisoner. They handed him over to Cyrus.
stops.quote_source: The Nabonidus Chronicle, ii.1-4 (fall of Astyages, 550 BC)

stops.name: Pasargadae founded, the city on the field of victory
stops.campa: On the high plain where he broke the Medes, Cyrus founds his city, Pasargadae, and names it for his own tribe. Here rise the great gardens, the fourfold watered paradise, the pillared palaces with their guardian figures. Here he will keep the royal fire and here he will be buried. The Persian who was a herdsman's foster-son now sits where Astyages sat, King of the Medes and the Persians, master of the Iranian plateau, and turns his eyes west and south to the older, richer kingdoms of the world.

stops.name: Delphi, the oracle that ruins Croesus
stops.campa: In Sardis, Croesus of Lydia, richest of kings, who once asked Solon who was happiest of men and was told to call no man happy till he is dead, weighs war on the rising Persian. He sends gold beyond counting to Delphi and asks Apollo whether to march. The Pythia answers: if Croesus crosses the Halys he will destroy a great empire. He hears his own victory. He does not hear that the empire to fall may be his own. So the oracle, true and double-tongued, sends him east against Cyrus.
stops.quote: If Croesus should send an army against the Persians he would destroy a great empire.
stops.quote_source: The Delphic oracle to Croesus, Herodotus, Histories 1.53
